You do not need bumblebee or any of the other hacks anymore. The Nvidia drivers have handled this rather well for a couple of years, now.

That is a great misconception - bumblee needs to call 'bbswitch' which sends the ACPI signal to fully power off the NVIDIA device. Prime by itself does not handle this, and neither does the open source Nouveau driver. Even solutions which power off the PCI bus, but without sending the proper ACPI codes do not work.

That is why I made the video, because on this particular laptop if the NVIDIA card is on, you get about 20% battery life and it turns into a heater. There are a lot of misleading posts out there which mistakenly think they are saving power. You can also check out some of the struggles to get this right: https://github.com/Bumblebee-Project/bbswitch/issues/115

Also see: https://wiki.archlinux.org/index.php/bumblebee#Default_power_state_of_NVIDIA_card_using_bbswitch
My most recent rig is an MSI Dragon series with an M850 and piles of onboard and video ram. No problems at all when I loaded it up a year ago, and I have the power consumption stats to bear that out.

Ah I figured it out - you have a older model that still had separate hardware paths - for newer Optimus systems it's done by software using ACPI calls, which is why you see everything working appropriately.
I have four different Optimus rigs, and two of them are old enough to have had to use bumblebee in the past. Driver improvements have rendered that unnecessary.

Hey I know you were interested in getting the facts here - NVidia devs have confirmed what my video says: https://devtalk.nvidia.com/default/topic/957814/linux/prime-and-prime-synchronization/

" "Offload" attempts to mimic more closely the functionality of Optimus on Windows. Under normal operation, the iGPU renders everything, from the desktop to the applications. Specific 3D applications can be rendered on the dGPU, and shared to the iGPU for display. When no applications are being rendered on the dGPU, it may be powered off. NVIDIA has no plans to support PRIME render offload at this time."

That's talking about the automatic switching that occurs in the Windows version of the drivers for Optimus rigs. On Windows, the drivers will automagically detect when the high-power NVidia card is needed, and power it on/off accordingly. This feature is not available on Linux in any fashion, including Bumblebee. This is also not at all what we were talking about.
